subject: math
cluster: Work with radicals and integer exponents
description: Students use square root and cube root symbols to represent solutions to equations of the form $x^2 = p$ and $x^3 = p$ for positive rational $p$. They evaluate square roots of small perfect squares and cube roots of small perfect cubes exactly, recognize when a solution is irrational, and know that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.
subSkills: Evaluate square roots of perfect squares, e.g. $\sqrt{49} = 7$
Evaluate cube roots of perfect cubes, e.g. $\sqrt[3]{27} = 3$
Solve $x^2 = p$ and give both solutions $x = \pm\sqrt{p}$
Solve $x^3 = p$ and give the single real solution $x = \sqrt[3]{p}$
Evaluate square and cube roots of perfect-square/perfect-cube fractions, e.g. $\sqrt{\frac{9}{16}} = \frac{3}{4}$
Represent a non-perfect solution exactly with a radical symbol, e.g. $x = \pm\sqrt{5}$
Classify a square or cube root as rational or irrational
Know and justify that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational (and that the square root of a non-perfect square is irrational)

problemArchetypes.name: Solve with a fractional perfect square/cube
Classify rational vs. irrational
problemArchetypes.example: Is $\sqrt{2}$ rational or irrational? Answer: irrational, because $2$ is not a perfect square.

problemArchetypes.name: Real-world geometry application
problemArchetypes.example: A square has area $144$ square inches. Find its side length. Answer: $s = \sqrt{144} = 12$ inches (reject the negative root).

Easy.description: Direct one-step evaluation of a square root of a small perfect square or a cube root of a small perfect cube, or solving $x^2 = p$ / $x^3 = p$ where $p$ is a small whole-number perfect power.
constraints: Perfect squares with roots from $1$ to $12$ ($p \le 144$)
Perfect cubes with roots from $1$ to $5$ ($p \le 125$)
$p$ is a positive integer; no fractions
Single concept: either evaluate a root or solve a clean equation

Medium.description: Solving equations whose solutions are fractional perfect powers, classifying roots as rational vs. irrational, or representing a non-perfect solution exactly with a radical. Two reasoning steps.
constraints: Some equations have irrational solutions written as $\pm\sqrt{p}$ or $\sqrt[3]{p}$
Requires deciding rational vs. irrational and keeping the $\pm$ for square roots
May require simplifying a fraction or recognizing a perfect-power numerator and denominator

Hard.description: Multi-step word problems (geometry/volume), justification that a root is irrational, or comparison/ordering tasks that combine evaluation with reasoning about rationality and domain restrictions.
constraints: Area or volume context that requires setting up $x^2 = p$ or $x^3 = p$ and rejecting an inadmissible (negative) root
Requires explaining why $\sqrt{2}$ or another non-perfect-square root is irrational
May ask to compare two radical quantities or place a radical between two integers
Combines exact-radical representation with a contextual interpretation

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student multiplies the radicand by the index instead of taking the root
Student divides the radicand by the index instead of taking the root
Student gives only the positive root when solving $x^2 = p$
Student includes a negative root when solving $x^3 = p$ for positive p
Student confuses square root and cube root operations
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Computes $\sqrt[3]{64} = 8$ (the square root) instead of $4$, or $\sqrt{64} = 4$ (the cube root) instead of $8$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student calls a square root of a non-perfect square rational
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Claims $\sqrt{2}$ is rational because it can be approximated by a decimal like $1.41$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student takes the root of numerator and denominator incorrectly or only one of them
Student keeps a negative dimension in a geometry context
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reports a side length of $-12$ in. as a valid answer instead of rejecting it
